questions.stem: A regular rhythm at 58 has an upright P before every narrow QRS and a PR of 0.16. What is it?
questions.why: Every criterion for sinus rhythm is met except the rate. Under 60 makes it sinus bradycardia — significant only if it is producing symptoms.

options.t: Sinus arrest with a junctional escape taking over
options.why: Sinus arrest shows a dropped complex and a pause, neither of which is present here.

options.t: First-degree AV block, given the slow rate
options.why: First-degree block requires a PR longer than 0.20; this one is normal.

options.t: Junctional escape rhythm, which also runs in the 40s to 60s
options.why: A junctional rhythm has no upright P wave preceding the QRS in lead II.

questions.stem: A rhythm strip shows P-QRS-T complexes whose R-R interval lengthens and shortens with the patient's breathing. What is this?
questions.why: Sinus arrhythmia is a normal variant, especially in children and young adults. Rate rises with inspiration and falls with expiration as vagal tone shifts — every complex is otherwise a normal sinus beat.

options.why: Wenckebach drops a QRS; nothing is dropped here.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate
options.why: Fibrillation has no discernible P waves and no pattern to the irregularity.
Wandering pacemaker changes P wave shape from beat to beat; here they are identical.

questions.stem: How do you tell sinus arrest from a sinus block on a strip?
questions.why: In sinus block the node fires on time but the impulse does not exit, so the missed beat leaves a pause that is an exact multiple of the cycle. In sinus arrest the node itself fails and the pause has no such relationship.

options.t: Arrest is symptomatic while a block is silent
options.why: Whether a patient has symptoms depends on the length of the pause, not on the label.

options.t: Only arrest is followed by an escape beat
options.why: Either may be followed by an escape beat if the pause runs long.

options.t: A block has a wide QRS, while arrest keeps the QRS narrow
options.why: Both are supraventricular problems and leave the QRS narrow.

options.t: In a block the pause is an exact multiple of the R-R

questions.stem: What identifies a premature atrial contraction on a strip?
questions.why: A PAC starts in an ectopic atrial focus, so it arrives early and its P wave looks different from the sinus P. Because it still travels the normal path below the atria, the QRS stays narrow.

options.t: An early, oddly shaped P with a narrow QRS
A P wave with no QRS following it at all
options.why: A non-conducted P describes a dropped beat or a blocked PAC.

options.t: An early wide QRS with no preceding P wave
options.why: That describes a premature ventricular contraction.

options.t: A late beat after a pause, at a slower intrinsic rate
options.why: A beat arriving late after a pause is an escape beat, not a premature one.

questions.stem: A PAC is usually followed by a non-compensatory pause. Why?
questions.why: A PAC discharges the SA node and restarts its cycle, so the following P arrives sooner than expected. A PVC does not reach the SA node, which is why it is followed by a full compensatory pause instead.

options.t: It fails to conduct, so a full cycle is skipped entirely
options.why: A conducted PAC produces a QRS; a blocked one is a separate finding.

options.t: The AV node holds the next impulse until it recovers
options.why: Nodal recovery affects the PR interval rather than the timing of the following sinus beat.

options.t: It arrives so early that the ventricles cannot respond
options.why: The ventricles do respond — that is the narrow QRS you see with it.

options.t: It resets the SA node, so the next beat comes early

questions.stem: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at 160 shows no clearly visible P waves. What is the most useful label in the field?
questions.why: SVT is the umbrella term for a fast, regular, narrow rhythm from above the ventricles when you cannot identify the atrial activity. Naming the exact mechanism matters far less than the QRS width and the patient's stability.

options.t: Sinus tachycardia with buried P waves
options.why: Sinus tach is possible at 160, but a P you cannot find leaves the origin unproven.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
options.why: Atrial fibrillation is irregularly irregular; this rhythm is regular.

options.t: Ventricular tachycardia at an unusually narrow width
options.why: VT arises below the junction and produces a wide QRS.

questions.stem: What is the classic atrial rate in atrial flutter, and what does the baseline look like?
questions.why: Flutter comes from a re-entry circuit in the atria, usually near 300, producing the sawtooth flutter waves. The AV node blocks a share of them, so the ventricular rate is commonly a clean fraction — 150 at 2:1, 100 at 3:1, 75 at 4:1.

options.t: About 150 to 250, with normal-looking P waves
options.why: That pattern fits atrial tachycardia.

options.t: About 400 to 600, with a chaotic wavy baseline
options.why: Those figures describe atrial fibrillation.

options.t: About 60 to 100, with flattened P waves
options.why: A normal atrial rate does not produce flutter waves at all.

options.t: About 250 to 350, with a sawtooth baseline

questions.stem: Which finding is most characteristic of atrial fibrillation?
questions.why: In fibrillation the atria quiver at 400 to 600 with no organized contraction, so the AV node conducts unpredictably. The absence of a pattern to the irregularity is the finding to hang the diagnosis on.

options.t: Wide QRS complexes at a rate near 150
options.why: A wide QRS points below the junction unless a bundle branch block is present.

options.t: A regularly irregular pattern that repeats every few beats
options.why: A repeating pattern suggests a block or a grouped-beating rhythm.

options.t: An irregularly irregular response, no P waves
A regular ventricular response with sawtooth flutter waves
options.why: Sawtooth waves with a regular response describe atrial flutter.

questions.stem: Beyond losing the atrial kick, what is the major risk of atrial fibrillation?
questions.why: Blood pools in atria that quiver instead of contracting, and clots that form there can embolize. That is why patients in chronic atrial fibrillation are usually anticoagulated, and why cardioverting one who is not carries real risk.

options.t: Degeneration into ventricular fibrillation without warning
options.why: Fibrillation of the atria does not propagate into the ventricles that way.

options.t: Direct damage to the AV node from the rapid impulses
options.why: The node handles rapid input by blocking impulses, which is protective.

options.t: Progressive widening of the QRS as the rhythm persists
options.why: QRS width reflects the ventricular conduction path and does not change with duration.

options.t: Clot formation in the stagnant atria and embolic stroke

questions.stem: An irregular rhythm at 110 shows at least three different P wave shapes. What is it?
questions.why: Three or more P wave morphologies means several atrial sites are competing. Under 100 that is wandering atrial pacemaker; over 100 it is multifocal atrial tachycardia, which is strongly associated with severe COPD.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with occasional visible P waves
options.why: Fibrillation produces no organized P waves of any shape.
Same varied P waves, but a wandering pacemaker runs at 100 or below.

options.t: Sinus rhythm with frequent premature atrial contractions
options.why: PACs interrupt an otherwise regular sinus rhythm; here no single focus dominates.

questions.stem: Where does the P wave appear if the junction fires and the atria depolarize backward at the same time as the ventricles?
questions.why: A junctional impulse travels up to the atria and down to the ventricles at once. Depending on which arrives first, the inverted P falls just before the QRS, just after it, or is buried inside it.

options.t: Upright and normal in front of the QRS
options.why: An upright P in lead II means the impulse came from the sinus node, travelling the usual direction.
That happens when the ventricles depolarize slightly first.
That happens when the atria depolarize slightly before the ventricles.

questions.stem: A regular narrow-complex rhythm at 80 has no visible P waves. What is the most likely rhythm?
questions.why: The junction's intrinsic rate is 40 to 60. When it fires faster than that but under 100, the rhythm is called accelerated junctional; above 100 it becomes junctional tachycardia.

options.t: Normal sinus rhythm with flattened P waves
options.why: Sinus rhythm by definition shows identifiable P waves.
A junctional escape runs at its intrinsic 40 to 60.
Junctional tachycardia is above 100.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a PVC from a PAC on the strip?
questions.why: A ventricular focus fires below the His-Purkinje system, so the impulse crawls through the myocardium — wide, oddly shaped, with no P in front of it and a T wave usually opposite in direction to the QRS.

options.t: The PVC arrives late rather than early in the cycle
options.why: Both are premature — an impulse arriving late is an escape beat.

options.t: It is wide and bizarre with no P in front
The PVC has an inverted P wave preceding it
options.why: An inverted P before a narrow QRS points to a junctional origin.

options.t: The PVC is followed by a non-compensatory pause
options.why: A PVC typically produces a full compensatory pause; the PAC gives the non-compensatory one.

questions.stem: PVCs of differing shapes on the same strip tell you what?
questions.why: Uniform PVCs share one focus; multiform PVCs mean several irritable sites. Multiform beats generally reflect a more irritable myocardium and warrant a closer look at oxygenation, electrolytes and ischemia.

options.t: The PVCs are being conducted through different bundle branches
options.why: The shape reflects where the beat starts, not which branch carries it.

options.t: The patient is moving and the tracing is distorted
options.why: Movement artifact distorts the baseline rather than producing well-formed complexes.

options.t: More than one ventricular site is firing
A single focus is firing at varying intervals
options.why: One focus produces one shape, however irregularly it fires.

questions.stem: Every other beat on the strip is a PVC. What is this pattern called?
questions.why: Bigeminy is every second beat, trigeminy every third, quadrigeminy every fourth. Two in a row is a couplet and three or more in a row is a run of ventricular tachycardia.

options.why: Trigeminy is every third beat.

options.t: A short run of ventricular tachycardia
options.why: Three or more consecutive PVCs make a run of VT.
A couplet is two PVCs back to back.

questions.stem: Why is a PVC landing on the T wave of the preceding beat dangerous?
questions.why: The R-on-T phenomenon lands a stimulus in the relative refractory period, where recovery is patchy. That mixture of ready and unready tissue is what lets a re-entry circuit start ventricular fibrillation.

options.t: The ventricles are fully refractory and cannot respond
options.why: If the tissue were fully refractory the impulse would go nowhere, which is the safe case.

options.t: Coronary filling is at its lowest point during the T wave
options.why: The T wave falls within systole, but the hazard here is electrical rather than perfusion.

options.t: Part of the myocardium has recovered and part has not
The T wave carries more voltage than the rest of the complex
options.why: The T wave is a low-amplitude deflection; voltage is not the issue.

questions.stem: A wide-complex regular rhythm at 180 in an unresponsive, pulseless patient. What is your action?
questions.why: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia is treated exactly like ventricular fibrillation: immediate defibrillation with CPR around it. The rhythm's name matters less than the absent pulse.

options.why: Synchronization needs an R wave to track and is for patients who still have a pulse.
Pacing addresses rates that are too slow, not a pulseless tachycardia.

options.t: Amiodarone 300 mg IV push before any shock
options.why: Defibrillation comes first in a shockable arrest; antidysrhythmics follow failed shocks.

questions.stem: The same wide-complex rhythm at 180, but the patient is awake, alert, and has a blood pressure of 128/76. What changes?
questions.why: Stability decides the pathway, not the rhythm name. Stable wide-complex tachycardia gets a 12-lead and an antidysrhythmic; unstable gets synchronized cardioversion; pulseless gets defibrillation.

options.t: The rhythm can be treated as supraventricular given the stability
options.why: Stability does not narrow a wide complex — a stable wide tachycardia is still treated as ventricular.

options.t: Nothing — the rhythm still calls for immediate defibrillation
options.why: Defibrillating a conscious patient with a pulse is both unsynchronized and unnecessary.
A stable patient is not cardioverted first, and sedation is given when cardioversion is needed.

options.t: There is time for a 12-lead, an antidysrhythmic, and consultation

questions.stem: A wide-complex rhythm at 200 twists around the baseline, its amplitude waxing and waning. What is it, and what treats it?
questions.why: Torsades — polymorphic VT with a twisting axis — is usually driven by a prolonged QT and low magnesium. Magnesium is the specific treatment; if the patient is pulseless, they still get defibrillated.

options.why: Monomorphic VT keeps a constant shape rather than rotating.

options.t: Atrial flutter with aberrant conduction — adenosine
options.why: Flutter is an atrial rhythm and adenosine does not produce this pattern.
Fibrillation has no organized complexes to twist, and the first treatment is defibrillation.

questions.stem: What separates an idioventricular rhythm from accelerated idioventricular rhythm?
questions.why: Both are ventricular escape rhythms with wide complexes and no P waves; only the rate separates them. Accelerated idioventricular rhythm often appears after reperfusion and is usually transient.

options.t: The QRS width, which is narrow in the accelerated form
options.why: Both originate in the ventricles, so both are wide.

options.t: The presence of P waves in the accelerated form
options.why: Neither has associated P waves; both come from a ventricular focus.

options.t: Whether the patient has a pulse
options.why: Pulse presence is a clinical finding and does not define either rhythm.

questions.stem: The monitor shows an organized rhythm at 70 but the patient has no pulse. What is this?
questions.why: PEA is an electrical rhythm without mechanical output. The rhythm is not the problem to fix; the cause is, which is what the Hs and Ts exist to work through.

options.t: A false reading requiring a lead change
options.why: The tracing is genuine — the failure is mechanical, not electrical.

options.t: Asystole with electrical artifact on the tracing
options.why: Asystole shows no organized complexes at all.
Fibrillation is chaotic and never organized.

questions.stem: Before treating a flat line as asystole, what must you confirm?
questions.why: Fine ventricular fibrillation can look flat in a single lead, and a shockable rhythm must not be missed. Check a second lead, confirm the leads are attached, and turn the gain up before calling asystole.

options.t: The rhythm in a second lead, plus leads and gain
That the patient has been down for more than ten minutes
options.why: Down time informs prognosis but does not confirm the rhythm.

options.t: That the capnography waveform has gone flat
options.why: Low EtCO2 supports poor perfusion but does not identify the rhythm.

options.t: That a 12-lead has been recorded and printed
options.why: A 12-lead is not part of confirming asystole during an arrest.

questions.stem: Which of the four arrest rhythms are shockable?
questions.why: A defibrillator depolarizes the myocardium at once so a normal pacemaker can resume. That only helps when there is disorganized electrical activity to stop — VF and pulseless VT.

options.why: Asystole has no organized electrical activity for a shock to reorganize.

options.t: All four, as long as the patient is pulseless
options.why: Shocking asystole or PEA offers no benefit and interrupts compressions.
Those are the two non-shockable rhythms; they get CPR and epinephrine.

questions.stem: Every P wave conducts, but the PR interval is a constant 0.28 seconds. What is this?
questions.why: First-degree block is a delay, not a true block — every impulse gets through, just late. A fixed PR over 0.20 seconds with no dropped beats defines it.

options.why: Type II drops beats with an unchanging PR — nothing is dropped here.
Wenckebach lengthens the PR progressively and then drops a beat.
Complete block has no consistent relationship between P waves and QRS complexes.

questions.stem: The PR interval lengthens beat by beat until a QRS is dropped, then the cycle repeats. Which block is this?
questions.why: Wenckebach is progressive fatigue at the AV node — each impulse takes a little longer until one fails entirely, then the node recovers and the cycle restarts. It is usually nodal and usually benign.

options.why: First-degree block never drops a beat.
Complete block shows P waves and QRS complexes marching independently.
Type II holds the PR constant and drops beats without warning.

questions.stem: Why is Mobitz II more concerning than Wenckebach?
questions.why: Type I is AV nodal and often responds to atropine. Type II is infranodal — the tissue below simply fails intermittently, it does not respond reliably to atropine, and it can drop into complete block abruptly. That patient needs pacing available.

options.t: The lesion sits below the node and can progress
It causes a longer PR interval before each dropped beat
options.why: The PR in type II is constant — that is what distinguishes it.

options.t: It produces a slower ventricular rate
options.why: Either block can run fast or slow depending on how many beats drop.

options.t: It occurs only in patients with an anterior infarct
options.why: It is associated with anterior infarcts but is not limited to them.

questions.stem: P waves march out at 80 and QRS complexes march out at 38, with no fixed relationship between them. What is this?
questions.why: Complete AV block means nothing crosses the junction. The atria run at their rate, an escape pacemaker runs the ventricles at its own, and the two are dissociated. Treatment is pacing — atropine rarely helps.

options.t: Sinus bradycardia with a first-degree block
options.why: That would show one P conducting to each QRS with a long but constant PR.

options.t: Atrial tachycardia with a variable block
options.why: A variable block still conducts some impulses; here none conduct at all.
In 2:1 conduction the QRS still follows a P at a fixed interval.

questions.stem: In third-degree block, what does the width of the escape QRS tell you?
questions.why: A narrow escape means a junctional pacemaker at 40 to 60 — comparatively stable. A wide escape means a ventricular pacemaker at 20 to 40, slower and far less reliable. The wide one is the more urgent patient.

options.t: How long the patient has been in the block
options.why: Duration does not change where the escape focus is.

options.t: Whether the block will respond to atropine
options.why: Atropine acts at the AV node, so the QRS width does not predict a response.

options.t: How far down the escape pacemaker sits
The severity of the underlying infarct
options.why: Infarct size is not read from the escape complex.

questions.stem: A strip shows sharp vertical spikes each followed by a wide QRS. What is happening?
questions.why: A spike followed by a wide QRS is ventricular capture — the pacer fired and the ventricle answered. Spikes without complexes are failure to capture; spikes landing where they should not be are failure to sense.

options.t: A pacemaker is capturing the ventricle
Electrical artifact is being mistaken for pacer spikes
options.why: Artifact does not produce a wide QRS in a consistent relationship to each spike.

options.t: The pacemaker is failing to sense the patient's own beats
options.why: Failure to sense puts spikes in the middle of intrinsic complexes, at inappropriate times.

options.t: The pacemaker is firing but failing to capture
options.why: Failure to capture shows a spike with no complex after it.

questions.stem: A patient with a permanent pacemaker is in cardiac arrest with a shockable rhythm. How does the device change your defibrillation?
questions.why: Keep the pads at least 8 cm from the generator, or use an anterior-posterior placement, then defibrillate at normal energy. The device may need interrogation afterward — that is a hospital problem.

options.t: Deactivate the device with a magnet before shocking
options.why: A magnet changes pacing behaviour and has no place in an arrest.

options.t: Move the pads clear of the generator, then shock normally
Halve the energy setting to protect the pacemaker
options.why: Reduced energy risks a failed shock, and the pacemaker is not the priority.

options.t: Defibrillation is contraindicated with an implanted device
options.why: The patient will die without defibrillation; a device is not a reason to withhold it.

questions.stem: A patient's monitor shows a rate of 42 in an escape rhythm. They are awake, warm, dry and asking to be left alone. What guides your treatment?
questions.why: Bradycardia is treated when it is symptomatic — altered mentation, chest pain, hypotension, signs of shock, acute heart failure. A comfortable, well-perfused patient at 42 is monitored, not medicated.

options.t: The rhythm's name, since an escape rhythm needs pacing
options.why: An escape rhythm maintaining adequate perfusion may need nothing but monitoring.

options.t: The QRS width, which determines whether atropine will work
options.why: Width informs where the block sits, but symptoms decide whether to treat at all.

options.t: Whether the slow rate is producing symptoms
The rate alone, since 42 falls below the treatment threshold
options.why: There is no rate number that mandates treatment independent of the patient.

questions.stem: You cannot decide whether a fast wide-complex rhythm is VT or SVT with aberrancy. How should you treat it?
questions.why: When you cannot tell, assume the more dangerous one. Treating VT as SVT can be lethal; treating SVT as VT is generally survivable — and a wide-complex tachycardia in an older patient with cardiac history is VT until proven otherwise.

options.t: With a trial of adenosine to see which it is
options.why: Adenosine as a diagnostic trial is a hospital decision, not the default field move.

options.t: By waiting to see whether the rhythm converts on its own
options.why: Waiting on an undifferentiated wide tachycardia risks deterioration.

options.t: As SVT, since aberrancy is the more common explanation
options.why: VT is the more common cause of a wide-complex tachycardia, particularly in older patients with cardiac history.

questions.stem: A patient in atrial fibrillation has a ventricular rate of 165 and is hypotensive and confused. What does the rhythm's duration change?
questions.why: In chronic atrial fibrillation, cardioverting can dislodge an atrial clot — a real concern for the stable patient. An unstable one is already failing, and restoring the rhythm takes priority over that risk.

options.t: Rate control is preferred over cardioversion in all cases
options.why: Rate control fits the stable patient; instability calls for cardioversion.

options.t: Cardioversion must be deferred until anticoagulation is confirmed
options.why: Deferring cardioversion in an unstable patient trades a possible stroke for a certain arrest.

options.t: Nothing urgent — instability drives immediate cardioversion
The energy setting must be reduced for chronic fibrillation
options.why: Energy is chosen for the rhythm, not for how long it has been present.

questions.stem: Match each AV block to its defining feature on the strip.
questions.why: The whole family is read from two questions: is the PR constant, and does anything drop? Those two answers separate all four degrees.
pairs: PR longer than 0.20, every beat conducts
PR lengthens progressively, then a QRS drops
PR stays constant, QRS complexes drop without warning
P waves and QRS complexes march independently
Every other P conducts, with no PR trend to read
The pause is an exact multiple of the underlying cycle

questions.stem: Match each rhythm to where the impulse originates.
questions.why: Origin sets QRS width, and QRS width sets treatment. Everything at or above the junction conducts normally and stays narrow; everything below it is wide.

questions.stem: A rhythm is regular at 150 with a narrow QRS and no visible P waves. Which underlying rhythm should you specifically consider?
questions.why: A rate parked at almost exactly 150 should always prompt a look for flutter waves, since 300 divided by two lands there. They often hide in the T waves — a different lead or a vagal maneuver can reveal them.

options.t: Third-degree block with a junctional escape
options.why: A junctional escape runs at 40 to 60, not 150.
That rhythm is wide and slower than this one.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid response
options.why: Fibrillation is irregular; a metronome-regular 150 argues against it.

questions.stem: How does fine ventricular fibrillation differ from coarse in what it tells you?
questions.why: Amplitude falls as myocardial energy stores deplete, so fine fibrillation generally means a longer downtime and a worse prognosis. Both are treated identically: compressions and defibrillation.

options.t: Fine indicates an underlying respiratory rather than cardiac cause
options.why: Waveform amplitude does not identify the cause of the arrest.

options.t: Coarse fibrillation requires higher defibrillation energy
options.why: Energy is set by the device's recommendation, not by waveform amplitude.

options.t: Fine usually means more time has passed since arrest
Fine fibrillation is not shockable and coarse is
options.why: Both are shockable — fibrillation is fibrillation.

questions.stem: A trauma patient is tachycardic at 130 with a normal-looking sinus rhythm. What should that finding prompt?
questions.why: Sinus tachycardia is almost always a symptom, not the disease — hypovolemia, hypoxia, pain, fever, anxiety. Fix what is driving it; the rate is the body's answer to a problem, not the problem.

options.t: A beta blocker to reduce myocardial oxygen demand
options.why: Blunting the compensation in a hypovolemic patient can collapse their pressure.

options.t: Synchronized cardioversion to slow the ventricular rate
options.why: Cardioverting a compensatory sinus tachycardia removes a response the patient needs.
Adenosine acts on re-entrant supraventricular rhythms, not on a sinus response to a stressor.

options.t: A search for the cause, not treatment of the rate

questions.stem: What rate range does the lecture give for sinus tachycardia?
questions.why: 101 to 180. Past 180 the rhythm is almost certainly not sinus in origin — that is the practical use of the ceiling.

options.why: 220 is above the ceiling given for a sinus-origin rate.

options.t: Anything over 100, with no upper limit
options.why: An upper limit is given, and rates above it point away from a sinus origin.
150 is not where the lecture caps sinus tachycardia.

questions.stem: How much R-R variation defines sinus dysrhythmia?
questions.why: Variation greater than 0.12 seconds. It commonly tracks respiration — faster on inspiration, slower on expiration — and in a young or healthy patient it is a normal finding.

options.why: 0.20 seconds is the PR interval limit, not the variation threshold.
Some variation is normal; the lecture sets a numeric threshold.
0.04 is one small box, well inside normal beat-to-beat variation.

options.t: More than 0.12 seconds between the longest and shortest cycle

questions.stem: A patient's rhythm alternates unpredictably between bradycardia and bursts of tachycardia. What is this called?
questions.why: Sick sinus syndrome — sometimes called tachy-brady — is a failing SA node that alternates between the two extremes. It is a common reason a patient ends up with a permanent pacemaker.

options.why: A wandering pacemaker changes P wave morphology while the rate stays near normal.
MAT is an irregular tachycardia with varied P wave shapes, not alternating slow and fast states.
Sinus arrhythmia is a gentle respiratory variation, not swings between brady and tachycardia.

questions.stem: How does the lecture distinguish coarse from fine ventricular fibrillation?
questions.why: The line is 3 mm of amplitude. Coarse means a heart with energy left in it and a better chance from a shock; fine usually means more time has passed since the arrest.

options.t: Coarse waves exceed 5 mm; fine waves are under 5 mm
options.why: 5 mm is not the boundary given.

options.t: Coarse has visible QRS complexes; fine does not
options.why: Neither has QRS complexes — that is what makes it fibrillation.

options.t: Coarse waves exceed 3 mm; fine waves are under 3 mm
Coarse is faster than 300 per minute; fine is slower
options.why: Fibrillation has no countable rate to compare.

questions.stem: Three PVCs occur back to back. What is this called?
questions.why: Two consecutive is a couplet; three or more is a salvo, also called a run of ventricular tachycardia. Bigeminy and trigeminy describe how often a PVC recurs in a pattern, not how many occur together.

options.why: Bigeminy is every other beat being a PVC, not consecutive PVCs.
A couplet is two PVCs in a row.
Trigeminy is every third beat being a PVC.

options.t: A salvo, or a run of VT

questions.stem: What are the rate ranges for junctional, accelerated junctional, and junctional tachycardia?
questions.why: The junction's inherent rate is 40 to 60. Above that it is accelerated junctional to 100, and junctional tachycardia beyond. A junctional PR interval, when a P is visible in front, measures under 0.12 seconds.

options.why: 60 to 100 is the accelerated range, not the inherent one.
The accelerated range runs to 100 and tachycardia starts above it.
20 to 40 and 40 to 100 are the ventricular escape ranges.

questions.stem: What ventricular rate does the lecture call agonal?
questions.why: Under 20 is agonal — a dying heart producing occasional wide complexes. 20 to 40 is idioventricular, 40 to 100 is accelerated idioventricular.

options.why: 20 to 40 is the idioventricular range.
40 to 100 is accelerated idioventricular rhythm.
Under 40 includes the idioventricular range, which is not agonal.

questions.stem: Above what heart rate does the lecture say cardiac output begins to fall?
questions.why: Past about 150 there is not enough diastolic time to fill the ventricles, so stroke volume falls faster than the rate rises. That number is the reason a rate above 150 gets your attention regardless of the rhythm's name.

options.why: Rates just over 100 are usually tolerated without a drop in output.
120 is still within the range where filling keeps up.
Output has already fallen well before 180.

questions.stem: Which rhythm does the lecture describe as the only true arrhythmia?
questions.why: Every other dysrhythmia is an abnormal rhythm. Asystole is the absence of rhythm entirely, which is the sense in which it is the only true a-rhythmia.

options.why: Fibrillation is disorganized electrical activity, not the absence of rhythm.
PEA has an organized rhythm; what is missing is the mechanical response.
Third-degree block has two independent rhythms, not none.

questions.stem: Which three findings define Wolff-Parkinson-White on the EKG?
questions.why: An accessory pathway lets the impulse bypass the AV node, so the PR shortens below 0.12, the initial upstroke slurs into a delta wave, and the QRS widens as a result. Lown-Ganong-Levine is the related picture with a short PR but no delta wave and a normal QRS.

options.t: A normal PR, a delta wave, and a narrow QRS
options.why: A normal PR means the impulse took the normal route with no accessory pathway.

options.t: PR over 0.20, a delta wave, and a narrow QRS
options.why: The PR in pre-excitation is short, not long.

options.t: PR under 0.12, a U wave, and a narrow QRS
options.why: The U wave is unrelated, and the QRS is widened by the delta wave.

options.t: PR under 0.12, a delta wave, and a widened QRS

questions.stem: How does Lown-Ganong-Levine differ from Wolff-Parkinson-White on the tracing?
questions.why: Both are pre-excitation syndromes with a PR under 0.12. WPW slurs the QRS upstroke into a delta wave and widens the complex; LGL leaves the QRS looking normal.

options.t: Short PR but no delta wave and a normal QRS
Normal PR with a wide QRS and no delta wave
options.why: That describes a bundle branch block rather than a pre-excitation syndrome.

options.t: Short PR with a delta wave and a normal QRS
options.why: A delta wave is the WPW finding, and it is what widens the QRS.

options.t: Long PR with a delta wave and a wide QRS
options.why: A long PR is the opposite of pre-excitation.

questions.stem: How should adenosine be given for reentry SVT?
questions.why: Use the IV site closest to the heart, push fast, chase it with 20 mL. Expect a short run of asystole — warn the patient. If the first dose fails, double it and repeat in one to two minutes.

options.t: Rapid push with no flush, followed by a fluid bolus
options.why: The flush is what carries the dose centrally; it is not optional.

options.t: Rapid push into the most distal vein available
options.why: A distal site lets the drug degrade before it arrives.

options.t: Rapid push at the site closest to the heart with a 20 mL flush
Slow push over one minute with a 10 mL flush
options.why: Its half-life is seconds — a slow push means none of it reaches the node.

questions.stem: About what proportion of reentry SVT does the lecture say vagal maneuvers will terminate?
questions.why: Up to a quarter. That is enough to be worth trying while the line and the drug are being prepared, and not enough to count on.

options.why: If vagal maneuvers worked nearly always, adenosine would rarely be needed.
10 percent understates it.
50 percent overstates what the lecture claims.

questions.stem: What must you check before performing carotid sinus massage, and how long should it last?
questions.why: A bruit means plaque, and massaging over plaque can throw a stroke. Auscultate first, then massage one side only for five to ten seconds.

options.t: Listen for bruits first; massage 30 to 60 seconds
options.why: The duration is much shorter than that.
The 12-lead is not the safety check, and 30 seconds is far too long.

options.t: Listen for bruits first; massage 5 to 10 seconds
Check blood pressure in both arms; massage 5 to 10 seconds
options.why: Bilateral pressures belong to the dissection workup, not this one.

questions.stem: What is the order of interventions for symptomatic bradycardia in this program?
questions.why: Atropine first, pacing when atropine fails or the block is low, then a dopamine or epinephrine infusion. Keep the SpO2 at or above 94 percent throughout.

options.t: Fluid bolus, then atropine, then pacing
options.why: A bolus is not the first step in the bradycardia algorithm.

options.t: Atropine, then transcutaneous pacing, then dopamine or epinephrine infusion
Transcutaneous pacing, then atropine, then dopamine
options.why: Atropine comes first when the patient has time for it.

options.t: Atropine, then dopamine infusion, then pacing
options.why: Pacing precedes the infusions in this sequence.

questions.stem: Which situation is an indication for transcutaneous pacing?
questions.why: Pacing is for the symptomatic slow rhythm that has not answered atropine, for high-degree blocks where atropine is unlikely to work, and as a standby in a patient at risk of deteriorating.

options.t: Any bradycardia below 60 regardless of symptoms
options.why: An asymptomatic slow rate is monitored, not paced.
A fast ventricular rhythm is cardioverted or treated with a drug, not paced.

options.t: Asystole that has persisted through three rounds of drugs
options.why: Pacing a long-standing asystole does not improve outcome.

questions.stem: A paced strip shows spikes with no QRS following them. What is this failure called?
questions.why: The spike is there, the myocardium does not answer. Failure to pace is a missing spike, failure to sense is a spike landing where the patient's own beat should have inhibited it, oversensing withholds pacing altogether, and a runaway pacemaker fires at a dangerously fast rate.

options.why: Oversensing makes the device withhold pacing because it misreads other signals as beats.
Failure to pace means the spikes themselves are missing.
Failure to sense means the device fires when it should have held back.

questions.stem: What is the most common type of SVT, and what causes it?
questions.why: AVNRT is the most common. The impulse loops back through tissue that has already recovered from the same impulse, so the circuit sustains itself. That is why adenosine — which briefly blocks the node — breaks it.

options.t: Wandering atrial pacemaker at a fast rate — the pacemaker site shifting
options.why: That describes MAT rather than nodal reentry.

options.t: Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction — a fixed reentry circuit in the atrium
options.why: Flutter is a distinct rhythm with sawtooth F waves.

options.t: Multifocal atrial tachycardia — several atrial sites firing
options.why: MAT is irregular with varying P waves and is not the most common SVT.

options.t: AV nodal reentrant tachycardia — an impulse re-entering tissue it already stimulated

questions.stem: In SVT, where do the P waves go?
questions.why: At 150 to 180 the T wave of one beat lands where the next P wave should be, so the P disappears into it. The QRS stays 0.11 seconds or less because the impulse still comes from above the ventricles.

options.t: They are obscured by the preceding T wave
They appear at a rate independent of the QRS
options.why: Independent P waves indicate a third-degree block.

options.t: They are inverted and follow the QRS
options.why: That is the junctional pattern, not SVT.

options.t: They are absent because the atria do not depolarize
options.why: The atria do depolarize; the P waves are simply buried.

questions.stem: Where can the inverted P wave appear in a junctional rhythm?
questions.why: The junction fires and the impulse travels two directions at once — down to the ventricles and backward up to the atria. Depending on which arrives first, the inverted P lands just before the QRS, inside it, or just after.

options.why: That is one of three possibilities, not the only one.
It can also fall before or after.

options.t: Before, hidden within, or after the QRS

options.why: It can also precede the complex or hide inside it.

questions.stem: In third-degree AV block, what rates do the P waves and the QRS complexes run at?
questions.why: The atria keep firing at their own rate while a ventricular escape pacemaker takes over below the block. Total dissociation: the P waves march out at their rate, the wide QRS complexes at theirs, and nothing connects them.

options.t: P waves 20 to 40; QRS 60 to 100 and narrow
options.why: That reverses the two — the atria keep the faster sinus rate.

options.t: P waves 60 to 100; QRS 20 to 40 and wide
Both at 60 to 100, simply out of phase
options.why: If both ran at the same rate there would be no dissociation to see.

options.t: P waves 60 to 100; QRS 40 to 60 and narrow
options.why: A narrow escape at 40 to 60 is junctional, which is a different picture.

questions.stem: A pacing spike appears in front of the P wave. Which chamber is being paced?
questions.why: Spike before the P means the atrium; spike before a wide QRS means the ventricle. A dual-chamber or AV sequential device does both. A demand pacemaker fires only when the rate drops below its set threshold.

options.t: Neither — that pattern is a failure to sense
options.why: A spike before the P is normal atrial pacing, not a malfunction.
A dual-chamber device produces a spike before each chamber it paces.
A ventricular spike lands in front of the QRS.

questions.stem: How do monomorphic and polymorphic ventricular tachycardia differ on the strip?
questions.why: Monomorphic VT has uniform tops and bottoms — one focus. Polymorphic VT varies in height, and torsades de pointes is the version that twists around the baseline. Both are cardiac arrest rhythms when there is no pulse.

options.t: Monomorphic complexes vary in height; polymorphic are uniform
options.why: That reverses the two.

options.t: Monomorphic complexes are uniform; polymorphic complexes vary in height
Monomorphic is regular; polymorphic is irregularly irregular
options.why: The difference is complex shape, not rhythm regularity.

options.t: Monomorphic is narrow; polymorphic is wide
options.why: Both are wide-complex rhythms.

questions.stem: Which conditions are listed as causes of pulseless electrical activity?
questions.why: PEA means organized electricity with no mechanical answer, so the question is always why. Shock of either kind, tamponade, massive PE, electrolyte disturbance, and overdose are the ones named — treat the underlying cause.

options.t: Coronary artery occlusion, listed as the single cause of the rhythm
options.why: PEA has many mechanical and metabolic causes beyond occlusion.

options.t: Electrolyte disturbance and drug overdose, with no mechanical causes named
options.why: Mechanical causes are on the list as well.

options.t: Shock, tamponade, massive PE, electrolytes, overdose
Massive pulmonary embolism and cardiac tamponade, and nothing else on the list
options.why: The list is longer than those two.

questions.stem: Which underlying causes of sinus tachycardia does the review sheet name?
questions.why: Hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, and low potassium or calcium. The treatment is the underlying cause, not the rate — the fast rate is the compensation, not the problem.

options.t: Hypoxia, metabolic acidosis, hypokalemia and hypocalcemia

options.why: Both of those slow the heart rather than speeding it.
Anxiety can cause it, but these are not the named causes.
Those are not the causes listed.

questions.stem: Work through this strip: regularity, rate, P waves, PR, QRS width. What is it?
questions.why: Regular, rate in the 70s, an upright P before every narrow QRS, and a PR inside 0.12 to 0.20. Every criterion for sinus rhythm is met.

options.why: The rate here is under 100.
Fibrillation is irregular and has no organized P waves.
A junctional rhythm would not show upright P waves in front of each QRS.

questions.stem: This strip meets every sinus criterion except one. What is the rhythm?
questions.why: Regular, upright P before every QRS, narrow complexes — sinus in every respect except a rate in the 40s. Treat it only if it is producing symptoms.

options.why: Sinus arrest produces a pause with a dropped complex; this rhythm is regular throughout.
Complete block shows P waves marching independently of the QRS complexes.
The upright P waves before each QRS place the origin in the sinus node.

questions.stem: Narrow complexes, regular, faster than 100. Name this rhythm.
questions.why: Regular and narrow at around 125, with P waves still visible ahead of each QRS. Sinus tachycardia is nearly always a response to something else — look for the cause rather than treating the number.

options.why: At this rate P waves are still identifiable, which points to a sinus origin.
There is no sawtooth baseline between complexes.
VT is wide; these complexes are narrow.

questions.stem: The R-R interval on this strip varies gradually. What is the rhythm?
questions.why: Every beat is a normal sinus beat — the cycle length just rises and falls, usually with respiration. It is a normal variant, common in children and young adults.

options.why: A PAC arrives early with a differently shaped P; these P waves are identical.
Wenckebach drops a QRS; nothing is dropped here.
Fibrillation is irregularly irregular with no P waves; here every complex has one.

questions.stem: Measure the PR interval on this strip. What is the rhythm?
questions.why: Every P conducts, so nothing is truly blocked — but the PR runs beyond 0.20 seconds and stays there. It is a delay at the AV node, and by itself it needs no treatment.

options.t: Junctional rhythm with retrograde P waves
options.why: The P waves are upright and precede each QRS.
The PR here is longer than the 0.20-second upper limit.
Wenckebach lengthens the PR progressively and drops a beat; this PR is fixed.

questions.stem: Follow the PR interval across this strip. What is the rhythm?
questions.why: The PR gets longer with each beat until one P fails to conduct, then the cycle restarts. That progressive fatigue at the AV node is Wenckebach — usually nodal and usually benign.

options.why: Type II holds the PR constant right up to the dropped beat.
Complete block shows no consistent relationship between the P waves and the QRS complexes.

options.t: Sinus rhythm with a non-conducted PAC
options.why: A blocked PAC is a single early P wave, not a repeating pattern of lengthening PRs.

questions.stem: The PR interval on this strip does not change, but complexes are dropped. What is it?
questions.why: A constant PR with beats dropping without warning means the lesion sits below the AV node. Type II does not respond reliably to atropine and can drop into complete block abruptly — have pacing ready.

options.why: The P waves march through on time — nothing about the sinus node has failed.
First-degree block never drops a beat.
Type I lengthens the PR before the drop; this one is constant.

questions.stem: Compare the P wave rate to the QRS rate on this strip. What is the rhythm?
questions.why: The P waves march at their own rate and the QRS complexes march at a slower one, with no fixed relationship. Nothing is crossing the junction — this needs pacing, and atropine rarely helps.

options.why: A junctional escape produces a narrow QRS, and it would not leave P waves dissociated.
An idioventricular rhythm has no atrial activity; here P waves are marching through.

options.t: Second-degree AV block, type II with 2:1 conduction
options.why: In 2:1 conduction each conducted P sits a fixed distance ahead of its QRS.

questions.stem: There is no pattern to the R-R intervals here and no P waves. What is it?
questions.why: Irregularly irregular with no discernible P waves and a wandering fibrillatory baseline. The atria are quivering rather than contracting, so the AV node conducts unpredictably.

options.why: Flutter has a sawtooth baseline; this baseline is only fibrillatory noise.
Sinus arrhythmia keeps a P wave in front of every QRS and varies gradually.
MAT shows three or more distinct P wave shapes; here there are no organized P waves at all.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm and its rate category.
questions.why: Same irregularly irregular pattern with no P waves, but conducting fast. At this rate diastolic filling suffers on top of losing the atrial kick, which is what makes patients symptomatic.

options.why: SVT is regular; this rhythm has no consistent R-R interval.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
Sinus tachycardia with artifact on the baseline
options.why: The irregularity is in the R-R intervals themselves, not in the baseline.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with a controlled rate
options.why: A controlled response sits under 100; this one is well above it.

questions.stem: What produces the sawtooth baseline on this strip, and what is the conduction ratio?
questions.why: A re-entry circuit in the atria fires near 300 per minute, producing uniform sawtooth waves. Here one in four gets through, so the ventricles run near 75.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with coarse fibrillatory waves
options.why: Fibrillatory waves are chaotic; these are uniform and regular.
2:1 conduction of an atrial rate near 300 would give a ventricular rate near 150.
The sawtooth waves march out regularly, which artifact does not do.

questions.stem: A regular rhythm just under 150 with a repeating baseline. Name it.
questions.why: A ventricular rate parked near 150 should always prompt a hunt for flutter waves, since 300 divided by two lands exactly there. They often hide inside the T waves.

options.why: 4:1 conduction of 300 would give a ventricular rate near 75, not near 150.
SVT has no organized atrial waves between the complexes.
Sinus tachycardia shows a single P wave per complex, not a continuous sawtooth.

questions.stem: Fast, regular, narrow, no atrial activity you can point to. What do you call it?
questions.why: Fast, regular, narrow, and with no identifiable atrial activity. SVT is the useful field label — the QRS width and the patient's stability drive treatment far more than the exact mechanism.

options.why: No P waves can be identified, so a sinus origin cannot be established.
VT produces wide complexes; these are narrow.

options.t: Atrial fibrillation with a rapid response
options.why: This rhythm is regular; fibrillation is not.

questions.stem: Note the inverted P waves before each narrow QRS. What is this rhythm?
questions.why: An inverted P before a narrow QRS means the impulse started at or near the junction and depolarized the atria backward. At 40 to 60 it is the junction's own escape rate.

options.why: Sinus P waves are upright in lead II; these are inverted.
An idioventricular rhythm has wide complexes and no P waves.
Accelerated means 60 to 100; this rate is in the 40s.

questions.stem: This narrow-complex rhythm is regular in the 80s with no visible P waves. What is it?
questions.why: The junction's intrinsic rate is 40 to 60. Firing faster than that but under 100 makes it accelerated junctional; the P wave is buried inside the QRS.

options.why: Junctional tachycardia is above 100.
An escape rhythm runs at the junction's intrinsic 40 to 60.
Sinus rhythm shows an identifiable P wave before every complex.

questions.stem: Wide complexes, no P waves, and a very slow rate. Name this rhythm.
questions.why: Wide complexes, no P waves, and a rate in the 20s to 30s — the ventricular Purkinje tissue escaping because everything above it has failed. It is the last pacemaker before asystole.

options.why: Asystole has no organized complexes at all.
Complete block shows P waves marching through; there is no atrial activity here.
The accelerated form runs 40 to 100; this is slower than that.

questions.stem: Wide complexes, no P waves, rate near 68. What is this?
questions.why: Same ventricular origin as an idioventricular rhythm, just firing faster than its intrinsic rate. AIVR often appears after reperfusion and is usually transient and well tolerated.

options.why: The unaccelerated form runs 20 to 40.
VT is faster than 100.

options.t: Normal sinus rhythm with a bundle branch block
options.why: A bundle branch block still has P waves in front of the complexes.

questions.stem: Wide, regular and fast, with every complex the same shape. What is it?
questions.why: Wide, regular, fast and monomorphic, with no P waves. What happens next depends entirely on the patient — pulseless means defibrillate, unstable means synchronized cardioversion, stable means a 12-lead and an antidysrhythmic.

options.why: SVT is narrow; these complexes are wide.
There is no sawtooth atrial activity, and the complexes are wide.
AIVR runs at 40 to 100; this is faster.

questions.stem: The QRS axis on this strip rotates around the baseline. What is the rhythm, and what treats it?
questions.why: Polymorphic VT with a twisting axis, usually driven by a prolonged QT and low magnesium. Magnesium is the specific treatment — and if the patient is pulseless they still get defibrillated.

options.why: This is a ventricular rhythm, not an atrial one.
Fibrillation has no organized complexes to rotate.
Monomorphic VT keeps a constant complex shape rather than twisting.

questions.stem: No complexes can be picked out of this tracing at all. What is the rhythm?
questions.why: Chaotic activity with no identifiable complexes, at reasonable amplitude. Coarse generally means a shorter downtime than fine. Either way the treatment is compressions and defibrillation.

options.t: Muscle artifact over an underlying sinus rhythm
options.why: No organized complexes can be found underneath the chaos.
Fine fibrillation has much lower amplitude than this.
Torsades has recognizable complexes that rotate; this has none.

questions.stem: Identify this rhythm and say why the distinction matters.
questions.why: Low-amplitude fibrillation is easy to mistake for asystole in one lead — which is why asystole must be confirmed in a second lead with the gain turned up. Missing this rhythm means missing a shockable arrest.

options.t: Coarse ventricular fibrillation — shock at higher energy
options.why: Amplitude does not change the energy setting.

options.t: A flat line from a disconnected lead — reattach and reassess
options.why: A disconnected lead produces a truly flat trace with no waveform.
There is disorganized electrical activity here, which asystole lacks.

questions.stem: A pulseless patient shows this tracing. What must you do before treating it as asystole?
questions.why: Fine ventricular fibrillation can look flat in a single lead, and a shockable rhythm must not be missed. Confirm in another lead, verify the leads are attached, and turn the gain up.

options.t: Obtain a 12-lead to confirm the absence of activity
options.why: A 12-lead is not part of confirming asystole during an arrest.

options.t: Confirm in a second lead and check the gain and connections
Deliver one shock in case it is fine fibrillation
options.why: Shocking asystole offers no benefit and interrupts compressions.

options.t: Give a fluid bolus and reassess in two minutes
options.why: Fluid may be indicated for a cause, but it does not confirm the rhythm.

questions.stem: One complex on this strip is early, wide and has no P wave in front of it. What is it?
questions.why: Early, wide, bizarre, with no preceding P wave and a T wave opposite in direction to the QRS. The full compensatory pause after it is the other giveaway — the sinus node was never reset.

options.why: A PAC is narrow and has an early P wave ahead of it.
A paced beat is preceded by a sharp pacer spike.
An escape beat comes late after a pause, not early, and is narrow.

questions.stem: Identify the pattern on this strip.
questions.why: Every other beat is a PVC, and they all look alike, so they come from a single focus. Bigeminy is worth noting and worth checking oxygenation and electrolytes over — it is not itself an emergency.

options.why: Trigeminy places a PVC every third beat.
Multifocal PVCs differ in shape; these are identical.
A run means three or more PVCs consecutively; here they alternate with sinus beats.

questions.stem: Two wide beats appear back to back on this strip. What is that called?
questions.why: Two consecutive PVCs make a couplet; three or more make a run of ventricular tachycardia. Couplets suggest a more irritable myocardium than isolated beats do.

options.why: Three or more consecutive PVCs make a run.
Bigeminy alternates a PVC with each sinus beat.
R-on-T describes a PVC landing on the preceding T wave, wherever it occurs.

questions.stem: What is happening on this strip?
questions.why: A sharp spike followed immediately by a wide QRS is ventricular capture. Electrical capture is what you see; mechanical capture is the pulse that matches the paced rate, and you need both.

options.t: A pacemaker is firing and capturing the ventricle
The pacemaker is failing to sense the patient's own beats
options.why: Failure to sense drops spikes at inappropriate points in the cycle.

options.t: The spikes are artifact over an idioventricular rhythm
options.why: Each spike sits in a fixed relationship to the complex that follows it.

options.t: The pacemaker is firing but failing to capture
options.why: Failure to capture shows spikes with no complex following them.

questions.stem: This patient has a pacemaker and no palpable pulse. What does the strip show?
questions.why: The device is firing on schedule but nothing follows the spikes — the myocardium is not depolarizing. That is failure to capture, and this patient is in arrest regardless of what the device is doing.

options.t: Ventricular fibrillation beneath the pacing artifact
options.why: There is no chaotic activity between the spikes.

options.t: Normal pacemaker function at the set rate
options.why: Regular spikes alone are not function — the myocardium has to answer them.

options.t: Asystole with no pacemaker activity at all
options.why: The spikes show the device is firing.

questions.stem: Using the six-second method on this strip, what is the ventricular rate closest to?
questions.why: Count the QRS complexes across the six-second strip and multiply by ten. Four to five complexes puts this in the 40s — bradycardic, and worth treating only if it is producing symptoms.

options.why: That would require eight complexes across the six seconds.
That would be roughly two complexes across the whole strip.
Counting the complexes across the strip gives fewer than six.

questions.stem: On this strip, what are the atrial and ventricular rates?
questions.why: Flutter's atrial rate sits near 300. Divide by the conduction ratio for the ventricular rate: 2:1 gives 150, 3:1 gives 100, 4:1 gives 75. Counting both rates separately is the habit to build.

options.why: The AV node is blocking half the impulses — the ventricles cannot keep up with 300.
A ventricular rate near 75 would mean 4:1 conduction.
The sawtooth waves are running at roughly twice the QRS rate.
